summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Bolívar stands under the national framework of Colombia. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Partner recognition and premise access are settled in the visitor's favour. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015; the first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country, with couples presenting a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises; a 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict.

Violence against trans people in Bolívar is documented, targeted and unresolved. Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader who had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement and joined its sixth symbolic return march of more than 500 survivors of sexual violence, was killed in Carmen de Bolívar in Bolívar on 22 May 2025; El Tiempo's investigation characterises the killing as a trans feminicide, and more than 19 days after her death the circumstances remained unclear. Her friend and fellow social leader Yirley Velasco remembers her as having taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality. A visitor in Bolívar therefore faces the risk of a named, publicly hunted social leader being killed with no established account of how or by whom.

The national figures a visitor would rely on are contested and, by the estimate of experts cited, unreliable. The Fiscalía's own database records 3,322 intentional homicides of people identified as LGBTIQ+ between January 2010 and May 2025; for 2024 it records 431 such homicides against about 160 reported by an NGO, a shortfall of 267, and one Fiscalía dependency's 2025 data shows 39 homicides against 156 in the policies-and-strategies base. Experts cited describe Colombia's information system as neither unified nor reliable, so state and civil-society counts diverge by a factor of roughly three.

The pattern the counting obscures is one of sustained lethal attack. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia' records one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours in 2025, with violence escalating along a continuum from discrimination through intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases) and threats (1,184 victims) to homicide and impunity. The report does not name Bolívar explicitly, but it documents the territorial expansion of this violence toward territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence alongside insufficient state response, and Bolívar sits within the coastal cluster flagged for that expansion and that weakest response. Nationally, 13 trans people were killed in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023. On 5 April 2025 a video showed Sara Millerey, 32, drowning in a creek outside Medellín in Bello, Antioquia, unable to swim with fractured legs, arms and hands; her mother Sandra Borja said "They killed her for being who she was", and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation.

Some of the targeting is organised rather than incidental. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, flyer campaigns announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work. The same armed-group and illegal-economy dynamics that Caribe Afirmativo identifies as driving the violence's territorial spread are present along the Bolívar corridor, though the inventory does not name a Bolívar-specific kill list.

Protection machinery exists at national level and has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Bolívar's exposure is best read as one department illustrating a national crisis rather than as an isolated local failure. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report maps a continuum of violence that expands toward territories hosting illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, and Bolívar falls inside the coastal cluster the report flags for that expansion and for the weakest state response. The Carmen de Bolívar killing is the concrete instance within that cluster, investigated by a national newspaper rather than resolved by local authorities.

The divergence between official and NGO counts is itself a risk factor for a visitor. A departmental homicide tally drawn from the Fiscalía database would return roughly three times the figure a human-rights organisation would return for the same year, and experts cited call the national information system neither unified nor reliable. Any expectation a visitor forms about local risk from a single official statistic is therefore built on a data base that the reporting itself describes as contradictory.

Comparatively, the national legal position remains among the most developed in Latin America, and it is the enforcement gap, not the statute book, that separates Colombia from jurisdictions where formal rights translate into protection. The UN Independent Expert's May 2025 assessment names exactly that disconnect, and the Special Jurisdiction for Peace's July 2023 gender-persecution indictments show the state conceding conflict-driven anti-LGBTI violence as a crime against humanity while killings continue.
localsOnly:
Residents of Bolívar use the same national route as any Colombian to amend a sex marker: a signed document before a notary, in force since the June 2015 rule change, with no judicial order, bodily inspection or psychiatric assessment required. National identification documents also carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025, so residents can hold documents that state their status openly without a court process.

Residents are also the constituency the contested homicide data is compiled for. The Fiscalía database lists 3,322 intentional homicides of people identified as LGBTIQ+ nationwide between January 2010 and May 2025, while an NGO's tally for 2024 is about 160 against the Fiscalía's 431; the gap affects how families, advocates and officials in Bolívar argue for resources and accountability in individual cases such as that of Nawar Jiménez.

Local organisers remain the visible point of continuity. Yirley Velasco, a social leader in Carmen de Bolívar, has continued to speak for Nawar Jiménez as someone who had taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality, and Jiménez had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement, joining its sixth symbolic return march of more than 500 survivors of sexual violence. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree and the May 2018 executive decree also bind national and local institutions on LGBTI obligations in education, health care, prisons, victims' proceedings, housing, work, recreation, sports and culture, which is the administrative basis residents use to press claims.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the circumstances of Nawar Jiménez's killing in Carmen de Bolívar on 22 May 2025 remained unclear more than 19 days after her death, and no source in the inventory records an arrest, a named suspect, a judicial outcome or an official cause. Whether the killing has since been investigated as a feminicide is not sourced here.

Unresolved: the current record references a comprehensive trans law in the Colombian legislature, but the inventory contains no source establishing its contents, its stage or its fate. Nothing in the sources confirms whether such a statute has been enacted, amended or abandoned.

Unresolved: Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report does not name Bolívar, so the department's placement within the coastal cluster flagged for territorial expansion and weakest state response is an inference from the report's geography and from the El Tiempo case, not a finding the report makes about Bolívar by name. No source in the inventory gives a Bolívar-specific count of LGBTIQ+ homicides, and the national 2025 rate of one killing every 32 hours cannot be apportioned to the department from these materials.

Unresolved: no source documents a Bolívar departmental ordinance, governor's decree or municipal measure on trans access, facilities or protection, and no source names a Bolívar-specific armed-group kill list of the kind documented in Guajira and Caquetá since March 2024.
